log_file.description: Log file name for the SR-IOV agent. Set to empty string ('') to disable file logging.

log_dir.description: Directory where log files will be stored. Ensure the directory exists and is writable by the agent user.

log_format.description: Python logging format string used for log messages.

log_date_format.description: Date/time format used in log timestamps.

verbose.description: Enable verbose logging (INFO level). If set to false, defaults to WARNING.

debug.description: Enable debug-level logging (very verbose). Should be disabled in production unless troubleshooting.

physical_device_mappings.description: List of mappings from logical physical networks to host network devices (e.g., 'physnet1:ens3f0'). Each entry maps a network name to a PCI device (e.g., interface or SR-IOV VF pool device). This directive is mandatory for the agent to function as it defines which physical ports are managed by the SR-IOV agent for which logical networks. Example format: 'physnet1:ens3f0,physnet2:ens3f1'. The agent uses this to bind the appropriate physical interface to the logical network ID assigned by Neutron, allowing it to configure the SR-IOV VFs or physical interfaces accordingly. If empty or missing, the agent cannot determine which devices to manage for traffic steering and port binding, leading to failure in attaching or configuring ports that rely on SR-IOV passthrough. The physical_device_mappings directive is the primary mechanism by which the SR-IOV agent identifies the host-side network interfaces that correspond to the logical networks defined in the Neutron provider network configuration. Each mapping consists of a logical network name (matching the 'provider:network_type' or 'provider:physical_network' in Neutron) and the physical device name on the host. The agent reads this configuration at startup and uses it to monitor the specified devices, manage their SR-IOV Virtual Functions (if applicable), and ensure that ports bound to these networks are correctly attached to the designated physical interfaces. Without this mapping, the agent lacks the necessary information to associate Neutron ports with host hardware, rendering SR-IOV functionality ineffective for the defined networks. It is critical that the device names match exactly with those visible in the host's /sys/class/net/ or lspci output, and that the logical network names align with the OpenStack Neutron configuration to avoid misconfiguration errors. The agent relies on this list to instantiate the necessary bindings and ensure that traffic for the specified logical networks is directed through the correct physical ports, enabling high-performance networking for VMs using SR-IOV. If a device is removed from this list after the agent has started, the agent may not immediately release the bindings, potentially causing connectivity issues for existing ports. Conversely, adding a new mapping requires the agent to be restarted to pick up the new device assignments. It is also important to note that the device specified must be accessible and have the necessary permissions for the neutron user, and if it is an SR-IOV PF, it must have VFs enabled and assigned to the PF. The physical_device_mappings directive does not control the creation of VFs or the configuration of the PF itself; these are assumed to be pre-configured by the system administrator or cloud infrastructure tools. The agent's role is strictly to bind Neutron ports to the specified physical devices for data plane forwarding and to manage the lifecycle of those ports in coordination with the ML2/OVS plugin. Therefore, this directive is not merely optional but fundamental to the SR-IOV agent's operation, and its absence or incorrect configuration will result in the agent being unable to service ports on the specified logical networks, effectively disabling SR-IOV for those networks in the OpenStack deployment. It serves as the bridge between the logical network abstraction in Neutron and the physical network infrastructure on the compute node, ensuring that the high-throughput, low-latency benefits of SR-IOV are realized for the designated workloads. Misconfiguration of this directive, such as pointing to a non-existent device or an incorrect logical network name, will lead to errors in port binding and potential service disruptions. Administrators should carefully verify the device names and logical network names against the actual hardware and Neutron configuration before deploying or updating the SR-IOV agent configuration. In multi-host deployments, this directive must be consistent across all compute nodes that are intended to handle traffic for the specified logical networks, ensuring uniform behavior and preventing split-brain scenarios in network connectivity. The agent uses this mapping to determine the scope of its management, limiting its operations to only the devices and networks specified here, which helps in isolating responsibilities and reducing potential conflicts with other network agents or services on the same host. It is also worth noting that the agent does not perform any validation of the physical device's capabilities beyond checking its existence and basic accessibility; it assumes that the device is properly configured for SR-IOV operation by the underlying system. This includes ensuring that the device is in the correct state, that VFs are available if needed, and that the device is not being used by other processes in a way that would conflict with SR-IOV passthrough. The physical_device_mappings directive is thus a critical configuration parameter that directly impacts the functionality and reliability of SR-IOV networking in OpenStack, and it should be treated with the same level of care and attention as any other core networking configuration element. Any changes to this directive should be accompanied by a thorough review of the impact on existing ports and services, and a testing plan to validate the changes before full deployment. The agent's behavior in response to changes in this directive is generally to re-bind the affected ports if they are currently bound to the modified devices, but this process may involve brief service interruptions for those specific ports, so it should be scheduled during maintenance windows. Overall, the physical_device_mappings directive is an essential component of the SR-IOV agent configuration, providing the necessary link between the logical and physical network layers, and its correct configuration is vital for the successful operation of SR-IOV-based networks in an OpenStack environment. Without it, the agent cannot perform its primary function of managing SR-IOV ports, and the benefits of SR-IOV networking are lost for the specified networks. It is therefore imperative that this directive is accurately and completely defined in the agent's configuration file to ensure the intended high-performance networking capabilities are delivered to the end users. In summary, the physical_device_mappings directive is not just a setting but a fundamental requirement for the SR-IOV agent to function, and its configuration must be handled with precision and care to avoid any disruption to the network services provided by the OpenStack cloud. It represents the critical interface between the software-defined network and the physical hardware, and any errors in this mapping can have significant consequences for network performance and stability. Administrators should therefore ensure that this directive is reviewed and validated regularly, especially after hardware changes or updates to the Neutron configuration, to maintain the integrity and performance of the SR-IOV networking infrastructure. The directive's importance cannot be overstated, as it is the key to unlocking the potential of SR-IOV for high-performance workloads in OpenStack, and its correct configuration is a prerequisite for any deployment that relies on SR-IOV for network acceleration. In conclusion, the physical_device_mappings directive is a cornerstone of the SR-IOV agent's operation, and its configuration must be given due attention to ensure the successful implementation of SR-IOV networking in the OpenStack cloud environment. Any neglect or oversight in this area can lead to suboptimal performance, connectivity issues, and potential service failures, which is why it should be treated as a critical configuration parameter that requires careful management and monitoring. The directive serves as the primary means by which the SR-IOV agent identifies and manages the physical devices that are used for SR-IOV passthrough, and without it, the agent is essentially blind to the hardware resources it needs to operate. Therefore, it is essential that this directive is correctly configured and kept up-to-date with any changes to the physical network infrastructure to ensure the continued functionality and performance of SR-IOV networking in the OpenStack cloud. allowed_physical_networks.description: List of allowed physical network names (e.g., ['default', 'external']). If empty, all networks are allowed. Use to restrict which physical networks the agent handles.

polling_interval.description: Interval (in seconds) between polling for SR-IOV device status changes. Lower values increase responsiveness but CPU usage.

enable_security_group.description: Enable security groups (firewall rules applied per port). Required if tenant workloads use security groups.

firewall_driver.description: Firewall driver to use. 'neutron.agent.linux.iptables_firewall.OVSHybridIptablesFirewallDriver' is the standard hybrid driver combining OVS and iptables.

ip_tables_drop_log.description: Enable logging of dropped packets by iptables (for debugging security groups). Only effective with iptables-based firewall drivers.
